prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I love your lips when they’re wet with wine And red with a wild desire; I love your eyes when the lovelight lies Lit with a passionate fire. I love your arms when the warm white flesh Touches mine in a fond embrace; I love your hair when the strands enmesh Your kisses against my face. Not for me the cold, calm kiss Of a virgin’s bloodless love; Not for me the saint’s white bliss, Nor the heart of a spotless dove. But give me the love that so freely gives And laughs at the whole world’s blame, With your body so young and warm in my arms, It sets my poor heart aflame. So kiss me sweet with your warm wet mouth, Still fragrant with ruby wine, And say with a fervor born of the South That your body and soul are mine. Clasp me close in your warm young arms, While the pale stars shine above, And we’ll live our whole young lives away In the joys of a living love.

outputs.L2:
I adore your mouth, still moist and crimson from wine,  
glowing with untamed longing.  
Your eyes enchant me when affection burns within them  
like an intense and ardent flame.  
I cherish the feel of your warm, fair arms  
wrapped tenderly around me,  
and the way your hair falls between us  
as your kisses meet my face.

I have no desire for restrained, emotionless affection,  
for the pale devotion of untouched innocence,  
for a saint’s pure serenity,  
or for a heart as blameless as a dove.  
Instead, offer me a love that gives without hesitation,  
one that laughs at the judgment of the world.  
When I hold your youthful, heated body,  
my vulnerable heart catches fire.

Press your warm, damp lips sweetly to mine,  
with the scent of red wine lingering on them.  
Speak with the fierce passion of the South  
and declare that both your body and spirit belong to me.  
Hold me tightly in your young, warm embrace  
beneath the glow of the faint stars,  
and together we will spend all our youthful years  
delighting in a love that is vibrant and alive.
outputs.L3:
The speaker passionately celebrates every aspect of the beloved’s physical beauty, admiring her lips, eyes, arms, hair, and kisses. These details convey an intense attraction rooted in physical closeness rather than distant or abstract admiration. The poem rejects cold, restrained, and idealized forms of love, presenting them as lifeless compared with the warmth and vitality of genuine desire.

Instead, the speaker praises a love that gives freely, without shame or concern for society’s judgment. Images of wine, warmth, fire, and physical intimacy symbolize the lovers’ overwhelming passion and the joy they find in one another. Their desire is not merely sensual, however; the speaker longs for a complete union of body and soul. Ultimately, the poem imagines a life devoted to love that is generous, joyful, physical, and fully alive.
outputs.L4:
The poem celebrates a form of love that is passionate, sensual, and fully alive. Through vivid images of wine, fire, touch, and intimate embrace, desire becomes something that can be tasted, felt, and physically experienced. Wine suggests intoxication and abandon, while fire evokes warmth, energy, and an irresistible force capable of consuming hesitation. The emphasis on closeness and touch unites emotional devotion with bodily desire, presenting them not as separate impulses but as essential parts of the same profound connection.

Against this vibrant vision, the poem rejects love that is cold, restrained, distant, or excessively idealized. Affection governed by caution and social convention appears lifeless because it refuses the risks and pleasures of genuine intimacy. The speaker has no interest in a love that survives only as an abstract ideal or that remains pure by avoiding physical expression. Instead, the poem insists that authentic love requires openness, vulnerability, and the courage to surrender oneself completely.

This surrender is not portrayed as weakness. It is a deliberate and joyful embrace of life. By giving themselves to one another physically and emotionally, the lovers discover a freedom that conventional judgment cannot provide. Their passion defies those who might condemn or misunderstand it, suggesting that personal experience is more truthful than restrictive social expectations.

The poem ultimately defines such wholehearted devotion as a “living love”: warm, active, embodied, and continually renewed through mutual desire. Because it engages both body and spirit, it offers not a fleeting pleasure but a lasting source of vitality and joy. In celebrating this union, the poem argues that love becomes most meaningful when it is accepted without shame, fear, or reservation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Share a passionate Victorian-era love poem about desire, wine-red lips, and rejecting cold, chaste affection.
counterfactuals.output:
### **No Winter Love**

Come not to me with snow-white vows,  
Nor offer hands that never burn;  
I crave no saint with placid brows,  
Whose measured heart will not return  
The fevered beat, the wild unrest  
That storms like summer through my breast.

Nay—bring me lips of wine-dark red,  
Rich as the cup at midnight drained;  
Let every cautious prayer be fled,  
And every timid pulse unchained.  
What worth is love, austere and pale,  
That dares not tremble, dares not fail?

I will not kneel at marble shrines,  
Nor kiss affection cold and chaste;  
Give me the flame that leaps and shines,  
Though dawn condemn what night embraced.  
One burning hour beneath your breath  
Is worth an age of bloodless death.

Then come—not crowned with lilies meek,  
But flushed with roses, fierce and fair;  
Let desire speak where words grow weak,  
And loose the darkness of your hair.  
For love that never risks the fire  
Is but the ghost of true desire.
